title: How Ventriloquism Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore ventriloquism: its origins as a spiritual practice in ancient Greece and Egypt (the "belly talker" etymology), its condemnation as necromancy and later Enlightenment-era debunking, the move to entertainment at the French court of Francis I, and the rise of dummies from Baron Dominion's nutcracker-jawed doll in the 1750s to Fred Russell's character-driven act with Coster Joe. They cover Edgar Bergen and Charlie McCarthy on radio, modern acts like Terry Fader, Darci Lynne and Jeff Dunham, the Vent Haven-style dummy museum in Kentucky, the scary dummy trope (Hitchcock's "The Glass Eye," Dead Silence), the myth of "throwing" the voice versus the ventriloquist effect, and practical tricks like replacing b/d/m/p/v/w sounds. The episode ends with a listener mail about the film 12 Angry Men and eyewitness testimony.

segments.title: Opening banter and Jerry's return
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with tour plugs and banter about Jerry's return, then describe their own brief attempts at ventriloquism as kids and their reactions to the documentary Dumbstruck.

segments.title: Definition and ancient origins
segments.summary: They define ventriloquism as speaking without moving the lips and distinguish it from puppetry. They explain that ventriloquists adjust volume and tone rather than literally throwing the voice, and trace early practice in ancient Greece and Egypt as a spiritual act by prophets and soothsayers.

segments.title: Belly talkers and religious condemnation
segments.summary: The term comes from Latin and Greek words meaning speaking from the belly. Ventriloquism was seen as necromancy and devilish under early Christianity, and practitioners were persecuted, before it moved toward entertainment.

segments.title: Enlightenment debunking and early court entertainers
segments.summary: Enlightenment thinkers explained ventriloquism as a trick, including a long book by Jean-Baptiste de La Chapelle. Louis Brabant, a sixteenth-century valet to Francis I, entertained the French court with comic voice work, a tradition of saying what the speaker could not.

segments.title: Dummies, Baron Dominion and Fred Russell
segments.summary: Dummies arrived in the 1750s with Baron Dominin's nutcracker-jawed doll, followed by lines of many dolls. Fred Russell, a late nineteenth-century British performer, reduced this to one dummy, Coster Joe, and wrote sketches around its character, earning him the title father of modern ventriloquism.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break and transition to the next topic.

segments.title: Edgar Bergen, radio and dummy culture
segments.summary: Edgar Bergen's radio ventriloquism act with Charlie McCarthy and Mortimer Snerd drew on character-driven jokes. Candice Bergen's childhood with the dummies is discussed, along with Bergen's will leaving money to Charlie McCarthy, and modern shock acts such as Otto and George and Jeff Dunham.

segments.title: Modern ventriloquism, museum and scary dummies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the ventriloquism revival with America's Got Talent winners Terry Fader and Darci Lynne, and the Kentucky dummy museum where dummies are preserved but not animated. They then cover the creepiness of dummies in pop culture, citing Hitchcock's The Glass Eye and Dead Silence.

segments.title: Ventriloquist effect and speech tricks
segments.summary: The hosts explain that ventriloquists do not throw their voices; the ventriloquist effect makes the brain link sound to moving lips. They describe techniques such as giving the dummy a distinct voice and substituting sounds for hard consonants like b, d, m, p, v, and w.

segments.title: Practice tricks, Porky Pig and Paul Zerdin
segments.summary: They discuss rewriting sentences to avoid hard sounds, the Elmer Fudd rule, and resonant vocal technique. They mention Paul Zerdin's old-school act and his America's Got Talent mask routine with Howie Mandel.

segments.title: Listener mail: Twelve Angry Men
segments.summary: A listener named Nathan writes in praising the film 12 Angry Men and its treatment of eyewitness testimony, prejudice and memory. The hosts thank him and sign off with contact information.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact info and social media links and close the episode.
